label: Invariant Polynomials with Matrix Arguments
notes: This appendix builds the algebra of symmetric functions that powers distribution theory on special manifolds. We start from the orthogonal action on symmetric matrices, find the invariants, and meet zonal polynomials and their multi-argument generalizations as the natural building blocks for hypergeometric functions of matrix argument.

label: Orthogonal Action and Invariants
notes: Everything begins with the congruence action of the orthogonal group on symmetric matrices. A polynomial that survives this action depends only on eigenvalues, hence only on the elementary symmetric functions or power sums. This is the algebraic fact that forces our polynomials to live on partitions rather than raw matrix entries.

label: Partitions Index the Theory
notes: Partitions of an integer k are the index set for the whole construction. Each partition is a weakly decreasing sequence summing to k, drawn as a Young diagram. The number of partitions controls how many independent invariant polynomials of a given degree exist, so partitions are the discrete skeleton beneath the matrix analysis.

label: Zonal Polynomials
notes: Zonal polynomials are the symmetric homogeneous polynomials indexed by partitions that diagonalize the orthogonally invariant Laplace operator. They expand the power of a trace and are normalized so their sum over partitions of k reproduces that power. They are the matrix-argument analogue of single-variable monomials.

label: The Splitting Identity
notes: The defining normalization says that the k-th power of the trace splits as a sum of zonal polynomials over all partitions of k. This identity is what lets every term-by-term computation of a matrix hypergeometric series proceed, because it converts ordinary scalar powers into the partition-indexed basis.

label: Hypergeometric Functions of Matrix Argument
notes: Hypergeometric functions of a symmetric matrix argument are defined by series whose general term is a zonal polynomial weighted by ratios of generalized Pochhammer symbols. Choosing the numerator and denominator parameter counts recovers matrix analogues of the exponential, the binomial, and confluent functions used throughout multivariate analysis.

label: The Generalized Pochhammer Symbol
notes: The generalized Pochhammer symbol attached to a partition is a product of ordinary rising factorials shifted along each part of the partition. It encodes the parameter dependence of every matrix hypergeometric coefficient, and its appearance is exactly why partitions, not just degrees, are needed to bookkeep the series.

label: Integral over the Orthogonal Group
notes: The central analytic tool averages an exponential of a trace over the orthogonal group with Haar measure. The result is a zonal-polynomial series in the eigenvalues of the two matrix arguments. This integral is the bridge from group symmetry to explicit special functions on the manifold of symmetric matrices.

label: Several Matrix Arguments
notes: To handle products and several matrices at once we need invariant polynomials of two or more symmetric arguments. These are indexed by several partitions together with a coupling, and they reduce to zonal polynomials when only one argument is active. They are the tool for moments of products and for noncentral distributions.

label: Stiefel Manifold Integrals
notes: Integrating an invariant polynomial of the projection over the Stiefel manifold yields a ratio that depends only on the eigenvalues of the argument. This is the mechanism behind densities of the matrix Langevin and Bingham families, where invariant polynomials supply the normalizing constants and the moment structure.

label: Worked Coefficient Computation
notes: We trace a single low-degree coefficient through the machinery. Listing the partitions of two, writing each zonal polynomial in power sums, and attaching the Pochhammer weights gives a concrete number. Doing this once removes the mystery from the abstract series and shows where each symbolic factor enters.

label: Why the Invariants Matter
notes: Invariant polynomials convert hard manifold integrals into convergent partition-indexed series, so distribution theory on Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds becomes computable. We close by mapping the pieces together: orthogonal symmetry forces invariance, partitions index the basis, zonal polynomials build the series, and group integrals supply closed forms.
